passage:
The email came at 4:10, while Rania was still in her school uniform at the kitchen table in their Sydney flat. Selective school test: not offered a place.
She read it three times. Then she closed the laptop very gently, as if it might break.
Mum had worked Saturday shifts at the bakery all year to pay for the Tuesday tutoring. Dad had stuck the practice timetable on the fridge. Her little cousins in Beirut had been told she was 'the clever one'.
Not clever, she thought. Just the one who costs them money. Every Saturday, for nothing.
Jin messaged: 'did u get yours??' She turned the phone face down.
When Mum came home and asked, Rania said she had a headache and went to her room. She lay there listening to her parents' voices in the kitchen and decided she was simply the stupid one in the family. That was the whole story now.

qa.q: Who had worked Saturday shifts at the bakery to pay for tutoring?
qa.a: Rania's Mum had worked Saturday shifts at the bakery all year.

qa.q: What does Rania's thought 'Just the one who costs them money' show about how she sees herself?
qa.a: She has turned one failed test into a verdict on her whole self, feeling ashamed and like a burden on her parents.

qa.q: What turning point is available to Rania at this stage?
qa.a: She could tell her Mum or a school counsellor what she is really thinking, so someone can help her see that one result does not decide who she is.

qa.q: How might Rania's Mum feel hearing that her daughter has 'a headache' and seeing her go straight to her room?
qa.a: Mum may sense something is wrong and feel worried and shut out, not knowing Rania thinks the tutoring money was wasted on her.

grounding: It shows a teenager who failed an entrance test deciding she is stupid and a cost to her family, turning one result into a verdict on herself.

passage:
The results sheet was pinned outside the coaching centre's office, and by six the corridor was packed. Nandini found her roll number and ran her finger along the row twice. Below cut-off. Well below.
Sunaina, her roommate from the hostel, found her on the staircase landing, sitting with her bag on her knees.
'Nandu? What did you get?'
Nandini didn't look up. 'Papa took a loan for this place, you know that? Two years' fees. And Ma tells everyone at the temple that I'll be the first engineer in the family.' She laughed, but it came out wrong. 'I'm the dumb one. I've always been the dumb one. I just made them pay to find out.'
Sunaina sat down beside her. The fan above them creaked. Down the corridor someone was cheering.
'I can't even call home,' Nandini said. 'What would I say? Sorry I'm a waste?'

qa.q: Who found Nandini on the staircase landing?
qa.a: Sunaina, her roommate from the hostel, found her.

qa.q: What is Nandini feeling when she says 'I just made them pay to find out'?
qa.a: She feels deep shame and believes that one bad result proves she is stupid and a burden to her parents.

qa.q: How could Sunaina support Nandini right now?
qa.a: Sunaina could stay with her, gently say that one test is not the whole of her, and help her talk to the centre's counsellor or call someone at home she trusts.

qa.q: What might it be like for Sunaina to hear her friend call herself a waste?
qa.a: Sunaina may feel shocked and worried, unsure what to say, and aware that Nandini needs more than a quick 'don't worry'.

grounding: It shows a teen at a coaching centre who failed a test deciding she is stupid and a waste of her family's money, with family expectations sharpening the shame.

passage:
"Vinita, Mummy's calling you for dinner."
"Tell her I'm not hungry, didi."
"You've been in here since the result came. What did it say?"
"I didn't clear it. The science school entrance. Everyone from my coaching batch got in except me and one other kid."
"Okay. That hurts. Come here."
"Don't. I'm just stupid, Swati didi. I've always been stupid. I only fooled everyone till now."
"One test decided that?"
"Papa paid for two years of coaching. Two years. And I gave him nothing back. I'm just a burden in this house."
Swati sat on the bed and took Vinita's cold hand. "Listen to me. You are not a burden. Hearing you say that worries me, so I'm not leaving you alone with it tonight. We'll tell Mummy how you feel, together, right now."
Mummy was already in the doorway. She came and sat on Vinita's other side. "Beta, a result is not you. Talk to me."

qa.q: How long did Papa pay for coaching?
qa.a: Two years of coaching.

qa.q: What does Vinita calling herself a burden show about how she feels?
qa.a: She feels deeply ashamed, turning one failed entrance test into a verdict that she is stupid and has let the family down.

qa.q: What turning point does Swati offer at this stage?
qa.a: She takes the burden words seriously, stays with Vinita and brings Mummy in that same evening instead of leaving her alone with the shame.

qa.q: What is it like for Swati to hear Vinita say this?
qa.a: Swati is worried and protective; hearing her sister call herself a burden makes her stay close and bring in their mother at once.

grounding: A teen who failed an entrance test turns it into a verdict that she is stupid and a burden, with family expectations weighing on her.

passage:
The day the medical entrance results came out, I didn't cry. I sat on the terrace and did the maths. Two years of coaching fees. Appa's extra shifts. Amma telling every relative I'd be the first doctor in the family. And I had missed the cut-off by a mile.
By evening I had decided three things: that I was stupid, that I had always been stupid, and that I was only a drain on the family.
Rehana aunty from downstairs found me there when she came up for her washing. I told her I was a waste of money. She didn't laugh or lecture. She sat on the water tank beside me and said, "Kalyani, one exam is not your whole life. Come, we'll go down to your amma together." She stayed while I told Amma, and Amma held me for a long time.
Four weeks later, I can see how one bad day swallowed everything else I knew about myself.

qa.q: Where did Rehana aunty find Kalyani?
qa.a: On the terrace, when she came up for her washing.

qa.q: What was Kalyani feeling as the family's sacrifices added up?
qa.a: Kalyani felt crushing shame and guilt, letting one result become a verdict of being stupid and a drain on the family.

qa.q: What turning point did Rehana aunty create that evening?
qa.a: She listened without lecturing, said one exam is not a whole life, and took Kalyani to Amma the same evening.

qa.q: How might Amma have felt hearing Kalyani that evening?
qa.a: Amma was probably shaken and sad to learn her pride had felt like pressure, and the long hug showed she cared about Kalyani more than any result.

grounding: A teen who misses an entrance cut-off decides they are stupid and a drain on the family, one result becoming a verdict on the whole self.

passage:
Counsellor's note, 12 June
Urmila, Class 10, came to my room at lunch. She had not cleared the entrance test for the science stream at the district school. She kept saying, "I'm stupid. I'm always the stupid one," and that her father, Tejas, had borrowed from his brother for her coaching. She said she is "just a burden at home". She would not look up.
I did not argue about marks. I told her that one test does not measure a whole person, that feeling this way was not her fault, and that I was glad she told me. Because she used the word burden, I stayed with her for the rest of lunch and called her father straight away. Tejas came to school at three. The three of us talked; he told her the loan was his choice, not her debt. Urmila cried, then asked about the other stream.
Follow-up: meeting with Urmila on Monday, call to the family tomorrow.

qa.q: When did Urmila's father come to school?
qa.a: At three.

qa.q: What does Urmila refusing to look up suggest about her feelings?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and worthless, treating one test as proof that she is stupid and a burden.

qa.q: What did the counsellor do at this stage, and why did it matter?
qa.a: The counsellor stayed with Urmila, didn't argue about marks, and called her father the same day, so the shame was met with care quickly.

qa.q: How might Tejas have felt hearing that his daughter called herself a burden?
qa.a: Tejas was likely shocked and sad, and wanted her to know the loan was his choice, not something she owed.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a teen turning a failed entrance test into a verdict of being stupid and a burden, with family expectations behind it.

passage:
Friday, 11 p.m.
The entrance results came at four. I didn't make the list. Not even the waiting list.
I keep thinking: I'm just stupid. All those coaching fees Papa paid, all of Mummy's early mornings packing my tiffin, and I've wasted it. I'm a burden, that's the truth. Rahul uncle's son got in on his first try, and everyone will ask on Sunday.
I didn't come out for dinner. Around ten Gautam bhaiya knocked and didn't leave when I said go away. He sat on the floor, and I told him what I'd been writing, the burden part too. He went quiet, then said, "Hansa, one test is not you," and went straight to get Mummy. She sat on my bed, held my hand and said nobody in this house thinks that, not for one second. She's sleeping in my room tonight. Tomorrow she wants us to see the school counsellor together.
I still feel stupid. But less alone.

qa.q: When did the entrance results come?
qa.a: The entrance results came at four.

qa.q: What does Hansa's word "burden" reveal about how Hansa feels?
qa.a: Hansa feels deeply ashamed and worthless, turning one failed test into a verdict on the whole self and the family's sacrifices.

qa.q: What made that night's response a good one?
qa.a: Gautam stayed despite being told to go and fetched Mummy at once; she reassured Hansa, stayed close all night and planned a visit to the counsellor.

qa.q: What might Gautam have felt hearing the burden part?
qa.a: He likely felt alarmed and deeply worried, which is why he went quiet and brought Mummy right away.

grounding: Shows a teen turning a failed entrance test into a verdict of being stupid and a burden, and family responding the same night.
